How a Feluqa CLI Is Structured ​

A Feluqa CLI is a console application: it has a named executable binary, a main.rs that starts Feluqa's console, and command handlers registered with that console. A command belongs to a console profile selected by the binary; it is not a standalone function.

The console is the runtime that selects a command, provides its arguments and execution context, and handles terminal input and output. A profile connects a binary name to the commands available in that console. Each command is a handler registered in the profile's source tree.

For this small CLI application, one simple structure is:

text
hello-cli/
├── Cargo.toml                # declares the `hello-cli` binary
├── build.rs                  # discovers command handlers
└── src/
    ├── main.rs               # declares the console profile and starts it
    └── commands/
        └── hello.rs          # the `hello` command handler

Cargo.toml gives the executable its binary name. The Feluqa CLI binary is named feluqa; a separate CLI application can choose a name such as hello-cli. The command folder is the project's choice. commands/ is a simple convention here, and the console profile points to whichever source folder the project uses.

The binary and its console entry point ​

The package manifest declares both the build script and binary:

toml
[package]
name = "hello-cli"
build = "build.rs"

[[bin]]
name = "hello-cli"
path = "src/main.rs"

Cargo integrates with specialized tools through build scripts instead of replacing those tools. It compiles and runs a package's build script just before compiling the package. The Cargo Book describes this build-script lifecycle. Feluqa's console scanner uses it to discover command handlers and generate their registration.

build = "build.rs" belongs under [package], because it configures the package's build script. It does not belong in [[bin]], which configures the binary target. Cargo can discover a root-level build.rs by convention; Feluqa declares the path explicitly so the manifest states that intent.

Before looking at the Rust files, one Rust term helps explain their first lines: Rust has a prelude, a set of commonly used names the compiler makes available without an explicit use. For example, ordinary code can often write Option, Result, String, and Vec without importing them. This is convenient, but it can hide where names come from and make generated code or macros depend on implicit imports.

Feluqa prefers explicit imports. #![no_implicit_prelude] suppresses the standard, extern-crate, macro_use, and tool preludes; the language prelude remains. Code explicitly imports or qualifies the names it uses, making dependencies and macro inputs easier to inspect and generated application code more predictable. See Program 0: Hello CLI for the library layers and an example using ::core.

The binary's main.rs declares which command profile belongs to it, then starts the console dispatcher. For example:

rust
#![no_implicit_prelude]
#![forbid(unsafe_code)]
#![deny(unused_must_use)]
#![deny(missing_docs)]

extern crate feluqa;
extern crate std;

use feluqa::console::{MakeConsole, Profile};
use std::process::ExitCode;

/// The console profiles compiled into this binary.
#[feluqa::console::profile_registry]
pub const PROFILES: &[Profile] = &[Profile {
    id: "hello-cli",
    name: "Hello CLI",
    binary_name: "hello-cli",
    commands_directory: "commands",
    header: "Hello CLI",
    launch_aliases: &[],
}];

fn main() -> ExitCode {
    MakeConsole::new(PROFILES).run()
}

build.rs asks Feluqa's build-time scanner to find the command handlers under the profile directory and generate their registration:

rust
#![no_implicit_prelude]
#![forbid(unsafe_code)]
#![deny(unused_must_use)]
#![deny(missing_docs)]

extern crate feluqa;
extern crate std;

// Root used to resolve each Profile::commands_directory.
const SOURCE_ROOT: &str = "src";
// Rust file containing the PROFILES declaration.
const PROFILE_SOURCE: &str = "src/main.rs";

fn main() {
    if let std::result::Result::Err(error) =
        feluqa::console::build::compile_profiles_from_source(SOURCE_ROOT, PROFILE_SOURCE)
    {
        std::panic!("could not compile profile commands: {error}");
    }
}

The normal feluqa dependency provides the console runtime; the build dependency enables the console command scanner. Cargo.toml declares the binary, build.rs generates command registration, main.rs starts the console, and the console profile owns the command handlers.

The planned CLI project scaffold will provide the manifest, dependency features, entry point, and build script. Its commands_directory value is relative to the source root (src in this example), so this profile discovers:

text
src/commands/hello.rs

That file is where the developer writes the command handler. The full hello.rs source and the command to run it are in Program 0: Hello CLI.
